meta.about: Curated metadata for dsn.html: the three Deep Space Network complexes and their dishes, spacecraft codes used by NASA's DSN Now feed, history, and an ILLUSTRATIVE sample snapshot used only when the live feed cannot be reached.

meta.elevationMaskNote: DSN antennas normally track above roughly 6 to 10 degrees elevation; 10 degrees is used here for the coverage drawings.

complexes.name: Goldstone
complexes.blurb: On the US Army's Fort Irwin range, 72 km north of Barstow. Operated for NASA by JPL.

dishes.note: The "Mars antenna": built at 64 m in 1966, enlarged to 70 m in 1988. Damaged in an over-rotation mishap in September 2025; NASA's investigation report (2026) puts its return to service years away.
The newest dish in the network, online in 2026.

complexes.name: Madrid
complexes.blurb: 60 km west of Madrid, run for NASA by Spain's National Institute for Aerospace Technology (INTA).

dishes.note: Enlarged from 64 m to 70 m in 1987.
Online in 2021; the first dish able to use every DSN band.

complexes.name: Canberra
complexes.blurb: In the Paddys River valley near Canberra, run for NASA by Australia's national science agency (CSIRO).

dishes.note: The only dish on Earth that can send commands to Voyager 2, far south of the celestial equator. Rebuilt electronics in 2020.

S.name: S-band
S.note: Oldest deep-space band; robust, lower data rates.

X.name: X-band
X.note: The workhorse of deep-space links since the 1970s.

Ka.name: Ka-band
Ka.note: Four times the frequency of X-band: narrower beams and faster data, but rain fades it.

K.name: K-band
K.note: Near-Earth high-rate band, used for example by the James Webb Space Telescope.

VGR1.name: Voyager 1
VGR1.mission: Grand tour of Jupiter and Saturn, now in interstellar space
VGR1.fact: The most distant human-made object. Its 23-watt transmitter is about as powerful as a refrigerator light bulb.

VGR2.name: Voyager 2
VGR2.mission: The only visits to Uranus and Neptune, now in interstellar space
VGR2.fact: It flew south past Neptune's moon Triton, so it now sits far below the celestial equator: only Canberra can see it.

NHPC.name: New Horizons
NHPC.mission: Pluto flyby (2015), then the Kuiper Belt object Arrokoth (2019)
NHPC.fact: Its whole Pluto data set took about 15 months to trickle home.

JNO.name: Juno
JNO.fact: Solar-powered at Jupiter, five times farther from the Sun than Earth.

MRO.name: Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter
MRO.mission: High-resolution imaging and relay for Mars rovers
MRO.fact: Has returned more data than all other Mars missions combined.

M20.name: Perseverance
M20.mission: Mars 2020 rover in Jezero Crater, caching samples
M20.fact: Talks to Earth directly at X-band, but sends most of its data up to orbiters first.

MSL.name: Curiosity
MSL.mission: Mars Science Laboratory rover in Gale Crater

MVN.name: MAVEN
MVN.mission: Mars Atmosphere and Volatile Evolution orbiter
MVN.fact: Measured how the solar wind strips Mars's atmosphere away.

M01O.name: 2001 Mars Odyssey
M01O.fact: The longest-serving spacecraft ever at Mars.

MEX.name: Mars Express
MEX.fact: Europe's first planetary mission; ESA's own ground stations share the load with the DSN.

TGO.name: ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter
TGO.mission: Sniffing Mars's atmosphere for trace gases, and relay
TGO.fact: Also relays data from NASA's rovers.

EMM.name: Hope (Emirates Mars Mission)
EMM.operator: UAE Mohammed bin Rashid Space Centre (MBRSC)
EMM.fact: The Arab world's first interplanetary mission.

CLPR.name: Europa Clipper
CLPR.mission: Dozens of flybys of Jupiter's ocean moon Europa
CLPR.fact: The largest planetary spacecraft NASA has built: its solar arrays span 30.5 m.

PSYC.name: Psyche
PSYC.fact: Carried a laser communications experiment that sent video from deep space.

LUCY.name: Lucy
LUCY.fact: Will visit more separate asteroids than any mission before it.

JWST.name: James Webb Space Telescope
JWST.mission: Infrared space observatory at Sun–Earth L2
JWST.fact: Sends about 57 gigabytes of science a day over 25.9 GHz Ka-band.

SOHO.name: SOHO
SOHO.mission: Solar and Heliospheric Observatory at Sun–Earth L1
SOHO.fact: Has found more than 5,000 comets, almost all by volunteers.

SPP.name: Parker Solar Probe
SPP.mission: Dives through the Sun's outer atmosphere
SPP.fact: The fastest object ever built: 192 km/s at closest approach.

STA.name: STEREO-A
STA.mission: Solar Terrestrial Relations Observatory, watching the Sun from the side
STA.fact: Drifted all the way around the Sun and passed Earth again in 2023.

ACE.name: ACE
ACE.mission: Advanced Composition Explorer, solar-wind monitor at L1
ACE.fact: Its solar-wind readings give about an hour's warning of geomagnetic storms.

WIND.name: Wind
WIND.fact: Still working after more than 30 years.

DSCO.name: DSCOVR
DSCO.mission: Deep Space Climate Observatory at L1
DSCO.fact: Photographs the whole sunlit Earth several times a day.

IMAP.name: IMAP
IMAP.mission: Interstellar Mapping and Acceleration Probe at L1
IMAP.fact: Maps the edge of the heliosphere from near Earth.

TESS.name: TESS
TESS.fact: Its orbit is in a 2:1 resonance with the Moon.

CHDR.name: Chandra X-ray Observatory
CHDR.mission: X-ray telescope in a high Earth orbit
CHDR.fact: Its mirrors are the smoothest ever made.

LRO.name: Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter
LRO.fact: Has photographed every Apollo landing site.

KPLO.name: Danuri
KPLO.fact: Carries NASA's ShadowCam, which sees into permanently shadowed craters.

CH2.name: Chandrayaan-2
CH2.fact: Its orbiter relayed for Chandrayaan-3's lander in 2023.

BEPI.name: BepiColombo
BEPI.fact: Needed nine planetary flybys to reach Mercury.

JUICE.name: JUICE
JUICE.fact: Will be the first spacecraft to orbit a moon other than ours.

HERA.name: Hera
HERA.mission: Survey of the asteroid pair Didymos and Dimorphos after the DART impact
HERA.fact: Will measure the crater DART punched in 2022.

ORX.name: OSIRIS-APEX
ORX.mission: Extended mission of OSIRIS-REx to the asteroid Apophis
ORX.fact: Delivered asteroid Bennu samples to Earth in 2023.

HYB2.name: Hayabusa2
HYB2.mission: Extended mission to the asteroid 1998 KY26
HYB2.fact: Brought samples of Ryugu home in 2020.

SOLO.name: Solar Orbiter
SOLO.mission: Close-up views of the Sun and its poles
SOLO.fact: Took the first pictures of the Sun's poles, in 2025.

history.title: Explorer 1 is tracked
history.text: In January 1958 the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) set up portable radio stations in Nigeria, Singapore and California to receive Explorer 1, the first US satellite. Goldstone's first dish followed that year.

history.title: The DSN is born
history.text: On 24 December 1963 NASA's deep-space tracking stations became the Deep Space Network (DSN), one network run by JPL for every mission.

history.title: The Mars antenna
history.text: Goldstone's 64 m dish, DSS-14, was finished in 1966; its first job was following Mariner 4 far beyond Mars. Canberra and Madrid got their own big dishes in the early 1970s.

history.title: Apollo 11
history.text: The first television from the Moon was received by NASA dishes at Goldstone and Honeysuckle Creek, Australia, and by the Parkes radio telescope. DSN dishes backed up the Apollo network, and in 1970 helped bring Apollo 13 home.

history.title: Voyager 2 at Neptune
history.text: All three 64 m dishes were enlarged to 70 m and arrayed with other radio telescopes to catch Voyager 2's faint pictures from 4.5 billion km away.

history.title: Voyager 2's lifeline rebuilt
history.text: Canberra's DSS-43, the only dish that can command Voyager 2, was off the air for most of 2020 for new transmitters and electronics.

history.title: An interstellar shout
history.text: In August 2023 a wrong command tipped Voyager 2's antenna 2° off Earth. DSS-43 sent a high-power 'shout' that reached it about 18.5 hours later and it turned back.

history.title: Voyager 1 recovers
history.text: From November 2023 Voyager 1 sent gibberish: a failed memory chip in its flight data computer. Engineers moved the code around the bad chip by radio; engineering data came back in April 2024 and all four science instruments by June.

history.title: The Mars antenna damaged
history.text: In September 2025 DSS-14, Goldstone's 70 m dish, was damaged when it rotated past its limits. NASA's 2026 investigation expects repairs to take years.

history.title: A new dish, and one light-day
history.text: Goldstone's DSS-23 joined the network in 2026. Voyager 1 shut down another instrument in April 2026 to save power, and on 18 November 2026 becomes the first spacecraft one light-day from Earth.
